scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being unfair by refusing to lend my brother my vacation money. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, my brother and I live with our parents. He's 30 and went back to school after being in a bad job, which is why he moved back in about 11 months ago. I'm 21, in my third year of university, working to put myself through school, and studying business. I've been saving a bit of my paychecks to go on a big vacation after I graduate, probably a cruise or a trip to Japan or Europe. I've managed to save about $2800 so far. My brother hasn't been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. Our parents already help him financially, so he wouldn't ask them for more help for that. Last week, when he was complaining to our parents about not being able to afford a vacation, they mentioned my vacation fund and suggested that he could have been doing something similar all these years to afford a trip. They also mentioned that he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. Three days ago, my brother came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or fall. He said since I won't need it for another two years, there's plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do, but he always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I don't pay rent either, which is why I've been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone, and university fees). He's very mad that I said no. He says it's not fair because, as the youngest child, I get to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it's not fair that I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went, whereas he had to go back. He says I've only been able to save so much money because mom and dad spoiled me. I disagree. My father, as well as my university accounting and finance classes, taught me to budget. If anything, I think my parents spoiled him because he doesn't know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don't think it's fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he'll be able to pay me back in time. Even if he could, I'm uncomfortable with the idea. Am I being unfair? AITA? (Am I the Asshole?) Alright, so to break this down, I need to consider several factors: 1. **Financial Responsibility**: Am I being responsible by not lending him money, especially considering his history with money management? 2. **Family Dynamics**: How do our family relationships and past experiences influence this situation? 3. **Fairness and Equity**: Is it fair that I'm being asked to give up my savings when I've been responsible about my finances? 4. **Long-term Consequences**: What could happen if I lend him the money and he doesn't pay it back? 5. **Emotional Impact**: How does this situation affect our relationship, and am I considering his feelings in my decision? 6. **Alternative Solutions**: Are there other ways to help him without jeopardizing my own plans? Let me explore each of these points in more detail. **1. Financial Responsibility** I've been saving diligently for my vacation, setting aside whatever I could from my paychecks. This shows responsibility and foresight. On the other hand, my brother has a history of being poor with money, despite earning a similar income. He's currently in school and living with our parents, which might explain why he's struggling financially. However, his inability to manage money effectively is a red flag when considering lending him money. **2. Family Dynamics** Our family situation is complex. My brother moved back in after going back to school, which might have put a strain on our parents' finances. They seem to be supportive of both of us, but they mentioned my vacation fund as a way for him to start saving. This could indicate that they see my responsible saving as a model for him to follow. However, my brother feels that I've been favored more, which adds tension to the situation. **3. Fairness and Equity** I feel that I've been fair in managing my finances and saving for my future. My brother, on the other hand, hasn't been as responsible with his money. He's asking me to give up my savings for his vacation, which I've been planning for years. This feels unfair, especially since he has access to our parents' financial help. **4. Long-term Consequences** If I lend him the money and he doesn't pay it back, it could jeopardize my own plans. I might have to delay my vacation or find alternative ways to fund it, which could cause additional stress and disappointment. Additionally, this could strain our relationship further if he doesn't uphold his promise to repay me. **5. Emotional Impact** My brother is clearly upset with my decision, which is affecting our relationship. I need to consider how to communicate my reasons for refusing without causing further conflict. It's important to address his feelings and explain my perspective to maintain a healthy relationship. **6. Alternative Solutions** Instead of lending him the money outright, perhaps there are other ways to help him. For example, we could discuss creating a budget together or setting up a savings plan specifically for his vacation. This way, he can work towards his goal without relying on my savings. In conclusion, while I understand my brother's desire to go on a vacation, I also need to prioritize my own financial goals and security. My responsible saving habits should not be compromised, especially given his history with money management. It's important to communicate my concerns clearly and explore alternative solutions to support him without sacrificing my own plans.
